report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Background: Adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) are typically operationalized as binary indicators (present/absent), collapsing heterogeneous exposure levels into a single count.
Whether preserving severity gradations improves the prediction of adult health outcomes remains an open empirical question with direct implications for research and clinical screening.

Objective: To systematically compare binary versus severity-weighted ACE operationalizations across multiple levels of data representation (item-level, domain-level, and sum scores), analytic frameworks (sum scores, exploratory factor analysis, item response theory, and penalized regression), and psychosocial outcomes in a perinatal cohort.
Method: Participants were 454 pregnant women recruited within a longitudinal project on early experiences and perinatal mental health.
ACEs were assessed using an expanded ACE/ACE-IQ-based instrument capturing both occurrence and severity of 30 adversity items across 17 domains.
Five outcomes were measured: depressive symptoms, prenatal psychosocial adjustment, resilience, social support, and benevolent childhood experiences.
Ten distinct ACE data representations were constructed.
Predictive validity was evaluated using repeated 10-fold cross-validation with honest estimation (factor models refit inside each training fold).
Results: Severity-weighted operationalizations consistently outperformed binary counterparts across all comparisons.
The largest advantage emerged when the severity-graded domain scores were retained as separated predictors.
Factor-based representations showed comparable predictive performance but poor structural adequacy and computational instability.
The severity advantage was consistent at every level of comparison.
Conclusions: Preserving severity information in ACE measurement was associated with greater out-ofsample predictive performance than binary scoring in this perinatal cohort.
These findings support considering severity-weighted, domain-specific scoring in future ACE research and warrant further evaluation of its potential utility in clinical screening.
Adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) have been established as one of the most robust predictors of adult physical and mental health outcomes since the landmark study by Felitti et al. (1998).

text.text: The original ACE Study assessed ten categories of childhood adversity and operationalized each as a binary indicator (present/absent), generating a cumulative count score ranging from 0 to 10.

This binary-count approach has become the dominant paradigm in ACE research, adopted in hundreds of subsequent studies and embedded in clinical screening tools worldwide (Hughes et al., 2017; Merrick et al., 2018).

text.text: Despite its widespread adoption, the binary operationalization has attracted increasing methodological criticism.
Collapsing ordinal or continuous severity information into dichotomous indicators entails a loss of potentially important variance (Lacey & Minnis, 2020; McLennan et al., 2020).

This loss of information is particularly significant because dose-response relationships between severity of adversity and health outcomes have been documented across multiple domains (Gilbert et al., 2009; Norman et al., 2012).

text.text: These decisions are not merely academic as they directly affect research conclusions about which ACEs are most strongly associated with health outcomes, how adversity relates to specific outcomes, and how screening instruments should be designed.

From a psychometric perspective, dichotomization of continuous or ordinal variables systematically reduces statistical power and attenuates effect sizes (MacCallum et al., 2002; Royston et al., 2006).

The present study provides a detailed, empirically grounded comparison of ACE operationalization strategies.

We systematically vary three dimensions: (a) binary versus severity-weighted scoring, (b) level of aggregation (item, domain, and composite), and (c) analytic framework (sum scores, exploratory factor analysis, item response theory, and penalized regression).
All comparisons use a common outcome set and a rigorous honest cross-validation framework designed to prevent information leakage.

We hypothesize that severity-weighted operationalizations will show better predictive performance than their binary counterparts at every level of analysis, and that the gains will be most pronounced when individual domains are entered as separate predictors rather than collapsed into a single sum.
>Method
text.formatted: <head n="2." >Method</head>

text.text: The sample comprised 454 pregnant women participating in a broader longitudinal research project [Blinded for review] on early experiences and perinatal mental health in Spain.
Initially, 502 women expressed interest and provided informed consent; however, 48 did not meet eligibility criteria or subsequently withdrew, resulting in the final analytic sample of 454.
Inclusion criteria were being pregnant at the time of enrolment, being 18 years of age or older, having sufficient proficiency in Spanish, and signing the informed consent form.
The exclusion criterion was not residing in Spain, to reduce potential differences related to access to pregnancy-related healthcare.
Data was collected between March 2024 and July 2025.
Participants were recruited through the Obstetrics Department of a public hospital in [Blinded for review], as well as through social media and women's associations.
In the initial phase, women completed a preliminary form accessible through a QR code, providing contact details.
Subsequently, a member of the research team contacted each participant by telephone to explain the study, confidentiality procedures, anonymization, and available support resources.
Women who agreed to participate signed the informed consent form digitally and received a personal code to anonymize their responses to the online questionnaire.
This study was approved by the Institutional Research Ethics Committee (approval number: PI 203/23) and was preregistered on the Open Science Framework (OSF).

text.formatted: <head n="2.2." >Instruments</head>

The instrument was built upon the original ACE framework proposed by Felitti et al. (1998), which included the 10 classic categories.

text.text: The instrument included 30 items organized into 17 thematic domains: emotional abuse, physical abuse, sexual abuse, emotional neglect, physical neglect, divorce/separation, exposure to domestic violence, household substance abuse, mental illness in the household, parental incarceration, parental absence, parental or family death, unsafe neighborhood, violent crime victimization, financial problems, homelessness, and bullying.
Items 1-9 were scored dichotomously (0 = absent,1 = present), whereas items 10-30 preserved ordinal severity information (0 = never,1 = mild/once,2 = moderate/sometimes,3 = severe/frequently).

Because ACEs were conceptualized as a cumulative index of heterogeneous adverse experiences rather than as a unidimensional reflective scale, internal consistency was not used as a primary psychometric criterion.

text.text: Five validated instruments assessed perinatal mental health and psychosocial outcomes.

Depressive symptoms were measured with the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9; Kroenke et al., 2001 Kroenke et al., , 2010)), nine items rated 0-3 (range 0-27), with higher scores indicating greater severity [α = .812].

Three covariates were included in all predictive models: maternal age, gestational age in weeks at assessment, and educational level.
Missing covariate values were imputed to the sample median.
Ten distinct data representations were constructed by crossing two scoring approaches (binary vs. severityweighted) with three levels of aggregation (item, domain, and composite).
Table 1 summarizes these operationalization strategies.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref> summarizes these operationalization strategies.

text.text: For binary representations, each item was scored as 0 (absent) or 1 (present).
For severity-weighted representations, dichotomous items (1-9) retained their 0/1 scoring, whereas ordinal items (10-30) retained their full severity range (0-3).

At the domain level, the binary score was defined as the maximum across constituent items, such that any non-zero item score resulted in a domain score of 1; the severity score likewise defined as the maximum severity across constituent items and then rescaled to the 0-1 range.
A clarification is warranted regarding the Felitti-10 severity representations at the domain and composite levels.

The severity-weighted versions reported here are possible because six of the ten Felitti domains (corresponding to abuse and neglect subtypes and domestic violence) included items with graduated frequency response options (items 10-30), whereas the remaining four (household substance abuse, mental illness, separation and incarceration) rely exclusively on dichotomous items (items 1-9) and are therefore identical under binary and severity scoring.
Consequently, any additional information captured by the severity-weighted Felitti-10 scores derives entirely from these six domains.
>Analytic Framework
text.formatted: <head n="2.4." >Analytic Framework</head>

text.text: The analytic pipeline proceeded in two stages.
Stage A screened candidate EFA solutions across representations, extraction methods, and numbers of factors using cross-validated R² from factor scores estimated on the full sample.

Stage B subjected the top candidates to honest cross-validation, refitting the entire factor model and outcome regression within each training fold and scoring held-out folds using training-set parameters only.

For each representation, EFA models were estimated using three extraction methods, minimum residuals (minres), principal axis factoring (PA), and maximum likelihood (ML), and numbers of factors ranging from K = 1 to K = 6 for all representations.

Parallel analysis was conducted as a descriptive reference but did not constrain the factor search grid, as it failed to converge for two of the seven representations (Extended-17 domain severity and Item ordinal-severity, both polychoric) and suggested values ranging from K = 4 to K = 7 where it did converge.

The appropriate correlation matrix was selected for each representation: tetrachoric for binary items, polychoric for ordinal and mixed binary/ordinal representations, and Pearson for continuous severity scores.
All models used oblimin rotation.
Items with extreme prevalence (endorsement < 5% or > 98%) were excluded.
text.formatted: Items with extreme prevalence (endorsement < 5% or > 98%) were excluded.

text.text: Factor scores were computed using the regression method (Thurstone, 1934).
text.formatted: Factor scores were computed using the regression method <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Thurstone, 1934)</ref>.

text.text: The top 22 candidates from Stage A were subjected to honest cross-validation.

In each of 10 repeats of 10-fold cross-validation, the entire EFA was refit on the training data (including prevalence filtering, correlation matrix estimation, factor extraction, and rotation), and factor scores for the held-out test fold were computed by applying the training-set weight matrix to test data standardized using the corresponding training-set means and standard deviations.
For each outcome, a linear regression (including covariates) was fit on the training fold and evaluated on the test fold.
This procedure ensures that all factor-model estimation and regression-model estimation occurs strictly within the training partition.
The two-stage screening procedure may introduce modest selection optimism, although all reported estimates derive from the honest cross-validation in Stage B.
Simple benchmarks.
Covariates only (serving as a lower-bound benchmark); Felitti-10 and extended-17 binary and severity sums; 10 and 17 domain indicators (binary and severity-weighted) entered as separate predictors.
Unidimensional 2PL models for binary items and graded response models (GRM) for ordinal severity items, at both item and domain levels.
For domain-level severity representations, the GRM was used only when the domain score retained ordered discrete categories; continuous 0-1 severity scores were not treated as ordinal IRT indicators.
IRT models were refitted inside each cross-validation fold (honest CV), analogous to the treatment of factor models.
Theta scores were estimated using expected posteriori (EAP) scoring.
LASSO regression was applied to domain-level indicators with nested crossvalidation for regularization parameter selection (Tibshirani, 2011).
text.formatted: LASSO regression was applied to domain-level indicators with nested crossvalidation for regularization parameter selection <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Tibshirani, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: LASSO serves as a supervised predictive reference representing the best achievable linear prediction with automatic variable selection, rather than as a formal upper bound.
Among honestly cross-validated factor models, a parsimony rule selected the model with the fewest factors whose mean R² was within Δ = .010 of the best-performing model.
Structural stability was assessed via split-half analysis (100 random splits), computing Tucker's congruence coefficient between independently estimated loading matrices.
Confidence intervals for cross-validated R² were computed using the t-distribution (based on the 10 repeatlevel mean R² values, with the standard error calculated across repeats).
This procedure was applied identically across factor models, benchmarks, IRT, and LASSO models to ensure comparability of all reported intervals.
All analyses were conducted in R using psych (Revelle, 2015), mirt (Chalmers, 2012), glmnet (Friedman, 2001), and custom cross-validation code.

text.text: The final sample included 454 pregnant women aged 22 to 47 years (M = 34.70, SD = 3.94).
Mean gestational age at assessment was 28.18 weeks (SD = 8.80).
Most participants were Spanish (95.8%), in a relationship (98.2%), highly educated (70.3%), and employed (91.6%).
Educational level was coded from 1 to 3 and showed a mean of 2.69 (SD = 0.50) (see Table 2).

text.text: Regarding clinical and contextual variables, 19.8% reported previous or current psychopathology, 70.5% had received psychological therapy, 15.9% reported financial or work-related problems, and 3.1% were involved in ongoing legal proceedings.

text.text: First, item-level representations consistently outperformed domain-level representations.
The item ordinal-severity/polychoric representation achieved the highest R² values across all extraction methods and factor counts (peak R² = .171 at K = 6, minres).
Second, severity-weighted representations outperformed their binary counterparts within each level of aggregation.
Third, R² generally increased with the number of factors, with diminishing returns beyond K = 4-5.
The Felitti-10 binary/tetrachoric representation yielded the lowest R² values (peak ≈ .100), whereas extended and severity-weighted representations generally showed higher values.
Twenty-two candidate models were promoted to Stage B.
>Stage A: Predictive Screening of Factor Solutions

text.text: The highest-performing factor model was the item severity/polychoric solution with minres extraction and K = 6 (mean R² = .184, 95% CI [.171, .200]).

However, applying the prespecified parsimony rule (Δ = .010), the selected model was the corresponding ML solution with K = 5 (R² = .175, 95% CI [.162, .189]), which was within .008 of the best-performing model.
Table 3 presents the top results.

text.text: The severity advantage was consistent at every level of comparison: • Sum scores.
Extended-17 severity sum (R² = .108) outperformed extended-17 binary sum (R² = .098; ΔR² = .010).
Felitti-10 severity sum (R² = .086) outperformed Felitti-10 binary sum (R² = .075; ΔR² = .011).
• Domain-level indicators.
Seventeen severity domain scores (R² = .175) substantially outperformed 17 binary indicators (R² = .133; ΔR² = .042).
Ten Felitti severity domains (R² = .132) outperformed 10 binary domains (R² = .088; ΔR² = .044).
• LASSO regression.
LASSO with 17 severity domains (R² = .191) outperformed LASSO with 17 binary domains (R² = .148; ΔR² = .044).
• Factor models.
The best severity factor model (R² = .184) outperformed the best binary factor model (R² = .165; ΔR² = .019).

The difference between severity-weighted and binary representations increased with the level of disaggregation: approximately .010 for composite scores, .019 for factor models, and .042-.044 for domainlevel representations.

text.text: The proportional improvement was largest for CD-RISC (54% gain) and DUKE (32% gain).
ACE representations showed higher out-of-sample predictive R² than the covariates-only model (R² = .001-.027), with the largest differences observed for severity-weighted approaches.
Figure 3 displays the loading matrix for the selected exploratory five-factor solution (51.9% total variance explained).

text.text: The five factors were interpretable at a descriptive level: Factor 1 (ML1, 17.1% variance) loaded primarily on ACE10, ACE11, and ACE12 and was labelled emotional neglect/lack of early nurturance.
Factor 2 (ML2, 11.8%) loaded on ACE15, ACE16, ACE14, and ACE5 and was labelled neglect and household dysfunction.
Factor 3 (ML3, 8.8%) loaded on ACE24, ACE20, ACE25, ACE26, ACE19, ACE21, and ACE23 and was labelled family violence, combining direct abuse and exposure to domestic violence.
Factor 4 (ML4, 7.7%) loaded on ACE27 and ACE29 and was labelled sexual abuse.
Factor 5 (ML5, 6.5%) loaded on ACE17, ACE4, ACE18, ACE6, ACE2, and ACE5 and was labelled household instability and socioeconomic adversity.
These factor labels should be considered exploratory and descriptive rather than evidence of a stable latent structure, given the fit and stability issues described below.
However, global fit indices fell below conventional thresholds: RMSEA = .586, TLI = -0.262, BIC = 27,918.

Furthermore, split-half stability analysis yielded a 100% failure rate: across the 100 random splithalf replications, Tucker's congruence coefficient could not be computed in any replication because at least one of the independently estimated factor solutions failed to produce a valid loading matrix.

Despite these limitations, severity-graded factor scores captured meaningful predictive information from item correlations, suggesting that ACE data contains exploitable covariance structure even when it does not conform to a simple-structure model.
For practical purposes, the computational instability advises against relying on the factor model as the preferred operationalization.

Consistent with our hypotheses, severity-weighted operationalizations outperformed binary representations across all levels of analysis, and the largest gains emerged when individual domains were retained as separate predictors rather than collapsed into summary scores.

This study provides a head-tohead comparison of binary versus severity-weighted ACE operationalizations across multiple levels of analysis, analytic frameworks, and psychosocial outcomes in a perinatal cohort.
The central finding is that preserving severity information consistently and meaningfully improves predictive validity.
This advantage is held across every comparison, sum scores, domain-level indicators, factor models, IRT latent scores, and penalized regression, and across all five outcomes.
The magnitude of the severity advantage varied systematically with model complexity.
At the sumscore level, the gain was modest (ΔR² ≈ .010), reflecting the limited capacity of a single composite to capture differential severity patterns.
At the domain level, the gain was substantial (ΔR² ≈ .042), representing to an 31% improvement.
The larger differences observed for domain-level representations suggest that preserving severity information may be particularly informative when distinguishing between specific types of adversity.

That is, different ACEs, and different degrees of exposure within the same ACE, carry non-equivalent developmental weight rather than functioning as interchangeable units within a single count (Briggs et al., 2021).

text.text: Beyond measurement convenience, this finding also has a theoretical explanation, as cumulative stress models propose that adversity affects health through the progressive dysregulation of physiological stressresponse systems, allostatic load, such that the degree and duration of exposure, not merely its presence, determine the biological burden (Danese & McEwen, 2012).

text.text: Consistent with this dose-graded view, cumulative-risk research has shown that the number and intensity of stressors, rather than any single categorical exposure, best predicts developmental outcomes (Evans & Kim, 2013).

text.text: A binary scoring scheme is, in effect, a truncation of this underlying dose-response gradient introduced earlier in this paper.
It retains information about whether a stressor occurred but discards information about how much.

Our results, that severity-weighted scoring outperforms binary scoring, and that the gain increases as more granular domainlevel information is retained, are consistent with what this framework would predict.

This dose-graded logic is particularly pertinent to the perinatal population as pregnancy is increasingly recognized as a period during which a mother's own history of adversity can shape offspring outcomes through cumulative biomedical and psychosocial pathways, including prenatal complications and postpartum maternal mental health (Gomis-Pomares et al., 2026; Rabasa et al., 2026), that appear to scale with the burden of the mother's early adversity rather than with its mere presence or absence (Madigan et al., 2017).

text.text: If the relevant transmission mechanisms are themselves graded, an ACE measure that discards severity information may systematically understate risk in exactly the population, pregnant women, where capturing that gradient has the most direct downstream relevance for maternal and infant outcomes.
This finding also has direct implications for ACE screening instruments.
If severity information is collected but collapsed into binary indicators for scoring, a substantial portion of the assessment's potential value is discarded (McLennan et al., 2020).

text.text: The additional cost of preserving severity during scoring is minor, no additional items, no additional respondent time, and minimal computational effort.

This is consistent with broader methodological evidence that dichotomizing continuous or ordinal variables reduces statistical power and can bias parameter estimates, regardless of the substantive domain (MacCallum et al., 2002; Royston et al., 2006).

text.text: Factor-analytic models did not clearly surpass simpler domain-level approaches.
The best factor model (R² = .184) only modestly exceeded unreduced 17 severity domains (R² = .175), while LASSO (R² = .191) slightly surpassed both.
Moreover, severity-graded factor models exhibited 40-52% failure rates in CV and poor global fit (RMSEA > .50, TLI < 0), and stability could not be verified.

text.text: Although the selected exploratory factor solution retained useful predictive information, its poor fit and lack of structural stability suggest that these factors should be interpreted cautiously and primarily as exploratory representations of ACE co-occurrence patterns.

This interpretation is broadly consistent with previous Spanish work on the ACE Questionnaire (Villanueva et al., 2026), which approached ACEs as concrete adverse experiences rather than indicators of a common latent construct.

text.text: The heterogeneity of adversity types, the mixture of binary and ordinal response formats, and low base rates of severe adversities combine to produce a correlation matrix poorly approximated by a small number of factors (Rhemtulla et al., 2012).

text.text: For practical purposes, researchers are better served by entering domain-level severity scores directly, possibly with penalized regression, than by attempting to extract factor scores from a poorly fitting model.
Binary/tetrachoric factor models were computationally stable (zero failures) and achieved reasonable predictive validity (R² = .165).
This stability makes binary models attractive where polychoric estimation is not feasible.
However, their R² was consistently below severity-weighted counterparts, confirming that computational convenience comes at an informational cost.
More broadly, these results suggest that the choice of ACE operationalization is not a minor technical  et al., 2025).

text.text: This convergence across instruments, populations, and cultural contexts suggests the severity advantage observed here is not specific to the ACE questionnaire or the perinatal population and situates the present findings as a predictive-validity counterpart to structural-validity evidence from other cultural settings.
Several limitations should be acknowledged.

First, the sample comprised pregnant women from an urban Spanish setting, mostly Spanish nationals and highly educated, limiting generalizability to other populations and to less advantaged sociodemographic groups.
Second, the sample size (N = 454), while adequate for cross-validation, constrained the stability of polychoric estimation.
Third, all measures were retrospective self-reports.
Fourth, the study examined concurrent predictive validity; longitudinal advantages of severity scoring remain to be established.
Fifth, the available severity gradations (four levels) represent a coarse approximation; finer gradations might yield further improvements.
Finally, candidate factor solutions were initially selected through predictive performance analysis before undergoing rigorous cross-validation.

Future studies could extend this approach by implementing fully nested cross-validation procedures, in which model selection and evaluation are repeated together at each resampling iteration and by testing severity-weighted models in independent validation samples.

For research: When severity information is available, severity-weighted domain-level representations should be preferred over binary ACE scoring, as they consistently showed greater predictive utility in the present study.
Researchers are encouraged to examine the robustness of findings across alternative operationalization of ACE exposure.

For clinical screening: Severity-weighted scoring may represent a promising alternative to traditional binary counts, although additional validation across population and settings is needed before clinical recommendation can be made.
The binary operationalization of adverse childhood experiences, while historically dominant, discards information about variation in adversity severity.

Across five outcomes in this perinatal cohort, severityweighted representations showed higher predictive R² than binary representations, with larger differences observed when individual domains were modeled separately.
Factor-analytic and IRT approaches did not consistently improve predictive performance beyond simpler domain-level severity representations.
These findings provide a rationale for further evaluating whether severity-weighted scoring could improve the utility of ACE assessment in clinical screening.
